items.stimulus:
In 2009, ecologist Mara Venn began cataloging mosses on four abandoned quarry walls. Unlike earlier surveys, she recorded not only each species but also the moisture and temperature at every two-meter grid point. By 2013, she had identified eighteen moss species, but she had not yet compared the walls statistically.

To test whether shade or mineral composition better predicted moss distribution, Venn’s team placed identical shade cloth over half of each wall in spring 2014. They expected shaded plots to support greater species richness because the cloth would reduce evaporation. Instead, after two summers, species richness declined in both covered and uncovered plots, while one moisture-loving species expanded only beneath the cloth. Because quarry managers had watered the uncovered walls during a dry spell, the team treated the 2014–15 richness comparison as inconclusive rather than as evidence that shade had no effect. They therefore shifted emphasis in 2016 from comparing richness to tracking how quickly plots recovered after conditions changed.

In that later phase, the team removed the cloth from half of the covered plots but left the remaining covered plots untouched, creating a recovery comparison. After one year, plots that had been uncovered throughout regained their original richness sooner than plots that had been shaded and then uncovered. The final report, published in 2021, recommended preserving naturally shaded walls but cautioned against creating shade abruptly. items.stem: Across all three wetlands, how many more moth crossings per period did the amber-lit sections average than the white-lit sections?
items.stimulus:
In spring 2023, ecologist Mara Venn studied whether the color of outdoor lamps affected moth activity at three restored wetlands. She selected Fen, Reed, and Marsh and installed paired lamps along paths at each site. Because the amber lamps were dimmer, the researchers conducted a second trial using white lamps lowered to the same 3,600-lumen output. In that trial, amber sections averaged 17 crossings per period and dimmed-white sections averaged 14, leading the team to report that lamp color, rather than brightness alone, likely accounted for most of the difference.

She had asked me to help move six citrus trees before the glasshouse was demolished. The smallest tree, a bitter orange, stood in a blue enamel tub whose rim was chipped on the western side. Rather than lift the tub, Elianor slid beneath it a canvas sling she had sewn from sailcloth.

She told me the sling had belonged to her brother Tomas, who had vanished at sea eleven years earlier. When I asked why she had not used the greenhouse cart, she pointed to its bent left wheel, damaged by a falling pane during the March storm. We carried the tree into the courtyard and set it beside a rain barrel marked 42. Before noon, Elianor had placed the other five tubs in a row along the brick wall, with the lemon tree at the end nearest the gate.

At twelve thirty, the demolition foreman, Pavel, telephoned to say that his crew would be delayed until Monday, giving Elianor two extra days. She did not celebrate; instead, she painted a white line around the place occupied by each tub. I assumed the marks indicated where the trees should remain, but she explained that they recorded the morning shadows so the trees could be returned to the same light after the move. When we left, she locked the glasshouse with a brass key hanging inside a cracked red teacup rather than on the empty hook beside the door.

items.stimulus:
In 1911, the Ashcombe Museum acquired a fifteenth-century Book of Hours whose opening miniature showed Saint Agnes holding a small cross. Because the miniature bore the bright colors and delicate gold leaf associated with the Flemish workshop of Willem Vrelant, the museum's first catalog assigned the entire manuscript to Vrelant's circle. That attribution seemed secure until conservators noticed that several pages had been trimmed more narrowly than the rest, suggesting that leaves had been removed before the book entered the museum. The missing leaves mattered because the surviving decoration was concentrated at the beginning and end, leaving the manuscript's central sections with little evidence about how many artists had worked on it.

A 1980s catalog revised the attribution, arguing that the book had been produced in Bruges but that its principal painter was an unidentified follower of Vrelant. Infrared examination later revealed underdrawings beneath the Saint Agnes miniature that differed from the finished contours: the first design placed the saint farther to the left and gave her a larger cross. Art historian Mara Ilyan interpreted this alteration, together with the uneven quality of the interior initials, as evidence that the opening miniature and the text pages had been made in separate campaigns. Her conclusion did not restore the original Vrelant attribution; instead, it divided responsibility between a highly skilled painter at the front of the book and a less accomplished workshop responsible for most of the interior.

The manuscript's borders provide a second, more limited clue about its production history. One set of borders contains tiny birds perched among blue thistles, a motif also found in two securely dated Bruges prayer books from the 1460s. Another set uses curling acanthus leaves but lacks both the birds and the distinctive blue pigment; these borders occur mainly beside the interior initials that Ilyan considered stylistically weaker. The current catalog therefore identifies the manuscript as a Bruges book assembled in stages, with an opening miniature related to Vrelant's circle, interior decoration by another workshop, and borders added or revised during the book's later completion.
